releases.title: Legal Bay Offers Year-End Pre-Settlement Funding for Plaintiffs Facing Holiday Expenses and Upcoming Bills
releases.body:
Plaintiffs with pending lawsuits may qualify for a cash advance to help manage holiday spending, college tuition, and other end-of-year financial obligations

CALDWELL, N.J., Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As the end of the year approaches, many families are preparing for holiday expenses, upcoming college tuition payments, and other financial obligations that can put added pressure on household budgets. For plaintiffs waiting for a lawsuit to settle, that pressure can be especially difficult. Legal Bay LLC, a nationwide provider of pre-settlement funding, reminds plaintiffs with pending lawsuits that they may qualify for a cash advance while their cases move through the legal process.

Unlike traditional loans, pre-settlement funding provides eligible plaintiffs with access to money based on the anticipated proceeds of a pending lawsuit. Funds may help cover everyday living expenses, holiday purchases, tuition bills, rent, utilities, medical costs, and other necessary expenses while a plaintiff waits for a settlement or court award.

Chris Janish, CEO of Legal Bay, says, "Waiting for a lawsuit to resolve can create financial uncertainty, particularly at a time of year when expenses tend to increase. Qualified plaintiffs may have options for accessing funds before their cases are resolved, giving them additional flexibility to manage their immediate financial needs without having to wait for the legal process to conclude."

To learn more about pre settlement funding, lawsuit funding, settlement loans, and legal funding options, please visit Legal-Bay HERE or call toll-free at 877.571.0405.

Pre-Settlement Funding for Year-End Expenses

Legal Bay provides non-recourse lawsuit funding to eligible plaintiffs involved in a variety of personal injury and other qualifying legal claims. Depending on the case, a lawsuit cash advance may help bridge the financial gap between current expenses and a potential future settlement.

Plaintiffs may seek pre-settlement funding for a range of year-end needs, including:

  • Holiday gifts, travel, and family gatherings
  • College tuition payments and education-related expenses
  • Mortgage or rent payments and household bills
  • Medical expenses and other essential costs
  • Everyday living expenses while a lawsuit remains pending

Pre-settlement funding is not available for every case. Approval and funding amounts depend on an individual review of the claim and the terms of the applicable agreement. Because non-recourse funding is generally repaid from a successful recovery, plaintiffs typically do not owe repayment if they receive no recovery, subject to the specific agreement.

Legal-Bay empathizes with those who've been grappling with the devastating effects of inflation and higher cost of living expenses that have impacted almost everyone. With the holidays fast approaching, everyone's financial state may seem a bit more precarious as they try to put together a memorable holiday season, shop for gifts, assemble meals, or travel to see family.

Legal Bay encourages plaintiffs who are experiencing financial strain while waiting for a lawsuit to settle to explore their options and understand the terms before accepting funding. An advance may provide short-term financial flexibility, but it can reduce the amount a plaintiff ultimately receives from a settlement.

How to Apply for Lawsuit Funding

Plaintiffs with an active lawsuit who need additional funds before the end of the year can contact Legal Bay to discuss whether their case may qualify for pre-settlement funding. The company works with plaintiffs and their attorneys to review eligible claims and explain the next steps in the application process.

To learn more about pre settlement funding, lawsuit funding, settlement loans, and legal funding options, please visit Legal-Bay HERE or call toll-free at 877.571.0405.

About Legal Bay LLC

Legal Bay LLC is a nationwide pre-settlement funding company that provides non-recourse legal funding to eligible plaintiffs with pending lawsuits. The company helps plaintiffs explore lawsuit cash advances to manage financial obligations while awaiting the resolution of their cases.

To apply right now for pre settlement funding, lawsuit funding, settlement funding, or legal funding, please visit Legal-Bay HERE or call toll-free at 877.571.0405, where agents are standing by.

CHEYENNE, Wyo., Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bechtel today announced a $1 million investment in Laramie County Community College (LCCC) and Western Wyoming College (Western) to expand skilled trades training and create new pathways into electrical and pipefitting careers in Wyoming. Bechtel also launched Build for More, a statewide campaign encouraging Wyoming students, and the families and educators who guide them, to consider the skilled trades as a first-choice career.
releases.title: Bechtel Invests $1 Million in Wyoming Skilled Trades Training, Launches 'Build for More' Campaign to Inspire the Next Generation of Craft Professionals
releases.body:
Investment funds tools, instructors, and new training pathways at two Wyoming colleges, including pipefitting program new to Wyoming higher education. The statewide Build for More campaign will encourage students to see the skilled trades as a first-choice career.

CHEYENNE, Wyo., Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bechtel today announced a $1 million investment in Laramie County Community College (LCCC) and Western Wyoming College (Western) to expand skilled trades training and create new pathways into electrical and pipefitting careers in Wyoming. Bechtel also launched Build for More, a statewide campaign encouraging Wyoming students, and the families and educators who guide them, to consider the skilled trades as a first-choice career.

The two efforts are designed to work together. The college investment expands real pathways into well-paying, in-demand careers, closer to the communities students call home. Build for More helps more young people discover those careers in the first place. New research commissioned by Bechtel found that Wyoming adults hold the trades in high regard, but many of the state's high school students have yet to consider them.

Bechtel's investment will support curriculum, instructors, equipment, and training facilities at both colleges. It includes a pipefitting pathway new to higher education in Wyoming and expanded electrical training that will allow more participants to complete their training in-state.

Bechtel announced the investment and campaign at a panel discussion at LCCC in Cheyenne with Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon, LCCC President Dr. Joe Schaffer, and Bechtel Senior Vice President Walker Kimball. The audience included students, educators, and business and community leaders. In addition to the colleges, the event was hosted in partnership with the Wyoming Innovation Partnership and the Wyoming Business Alliance.

Strong support for the trades, but a gap with the next generation

The research shows Wyoming adults value skilled trades careers. Eighty-nine percent view the trades favorably, 60% see them as a first-choice career, and 83% say the trades are respected in their communities. Compared with a college degree, more Wyoming adults also see the skilled trades as the better path for job stability, early-career earnings, and entering the workforce with less debt.

Students and teachers don't yet see the trades the same way. Nearly half of Wyoming high school students (47%) say they have never really thought about a career in the skilled trades. Only 20% plan to enter a trade program, vocational program, or apprenticeship after high school. Teachers are students' top source of career information, but only 28% of teachers see the trades as a first-choice career. Just 16% of teachers and 10% of students describe the trades as well paid.

"Skilled craft professionals build the infrastructure and energy projects that power communities, and the need for them keeps growing," said Walker Kimball, Senior Vice President, Head of Construction, Bechtel. "These are well-paying, stable careers that let people build a good life, often without leaving home. But it isn't enough to tell young people these careers are great. We have to give them more chances to see the work up close, then build real pathways to those jobs right here in the communities they call home. That's what this effort is about."

The partnership was developed with support from the Office of Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon and in collaboration with the Wyoming Innovation Partnership through the Wyoming Business Alliance. It builds on the state's ongoing work to bring industry and government together, expanding opportunities for Wyoming residents to train for and build careers in high-demand fields.

"Wyoming's workforce is one of our greatest strengths, and we want our people to have opportunities to build rewarding careers right here at home," said Governor Mark Gordon, State of Wyoming. "This investment brings together industry, education, and government to expand training for in-demand skills and create more pathways for Wyoming residents to build their futures in our state."

Expanding skilled trades training in Wyoming

At LCCC, Bechtel's investment will support electrical and pipefitting training, including curriculum, instructors, equipment, and dedicated training spaces designed to provide hands-on experience. The programs will prepare participants for employment and apprenticeship opportunities and connect graduates with local contractors and industry partners.

"Meeting the workforce needs of Wyoming requires strong partnerships between education and industry," said Dr. Joe Schaffer, President, Laramie County Community College. "Through Bechtel's investment, LCCC can expand access to high-quality, industry-driven training that equips students with the skills employers need today and into the future. These new opportunities allow students to earn nationally recognized credentials without leaving Wyoming, while helping build the skilled workforce that will support our communities, region, and economy for years to come."

At Western, Bechtel's support will expand electrical and pipefitting training through investments in faculty, equipment, and training capacity. The program also includes a mobile pipefitting training unit that will bring hands-on training and career awareness to rural communities across Wyoming. The unit puts both pathways and exposure into practice.

"This partnership allows us to expand high-quality, hands-on training and reach more students and workers throughout Western Wyoming," said Dr. Kirk Young, president of Western Wyoming College. "By bringing training closer to the communities we serve, we can help more Wyoming residents gain valuable skills and build careers right here in the state."

Build for More: Skilled trades as a first-choice career

Build for More is designed to reach students who may never have considered the trades, including those planning to pursue two- or four-year degrees, not only those already headed toward construction or technical careers. Because students say they rely most on parents and teachers for career guidance, the campaign will also engage the families and educators who shape students' choices.

Through digital storytelling, community engagement, and real-world exposure to construction careers, Build for More will show what the skilled trades offer: a strong start in your 20s with less debt, skills in long-term demand, room to advance, and the chance to build tangible things that matter.

Together, the training investment and the statewide campaign address both sides of Wyoming's workforce opportunity. They expand access to skilled trades training close to home and help more young people see these careers as worth pursuing.

About Bechtel

Bechtel is a trusted engineering, construction, procurement, and project management partner to industry and government. Differentiated by the quality of our people and our relentless drive to deliver the most successful outcomes, we align our capabilities to our customers' objectives to create a lasting positive impact. Since 1898, we have helped customers complete more than 25,000 projects in 160 countries on all seven continents that have created jobs, grown economies, improved the resiliency of the world's infrastructure, increased access to energy, resources, and vital services, and made the world a safer, cleaner place. 

Bechtel serves the Energy; Infrastructure; Manufacturing & Technology; Mining & Metals; and Nuclear, Security & Environmental markets. Our services span from initial planning and investment, through start-up and operations. www.bechtel.com

About Laramie County Community College

Laramie County Community College (LCCC) is a comprehensive public institution serving students from Wyoming and the region through affordable, high-quality academic, workforce, and transfer programs. With campuses in Cheyenne and Laramie, LCCC provides pathways to certificates, associate degrees, applied bachelor's degrees, and university transfer opportunities designed to meet the needs of students, employers, and communities. The College is committed to student success through innovative learning experiences, strong industry partnerships, and personalized support services. Since its founding in 1968, LCCC has played a vital role in developing Wyoming's workforce and expanding access to higher education.

Molly Edwards | medwards@bechtel.com

releases.title: The Princeton Review Reports Findings of Its "2026 Campus Mental Health Services Survey" Conducted in Partnership with the Ruderman Family Foundation
releases.body:
• 71% of college students surveyed say their school prioritizes mental health

• 49% of administrators surveyed say their institutions conduct regular wellness screenings

NEW YORK, Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Princeton Review®, one of the nation's leading education services companies, today reported findings of its third annual Campus Mental Health Services Survey. The 2026 survey is a part of a comprehensive initiative the company conducts in partnership with the Ruderman Family Foundation, an internationally recognized organization that works to end the stigma associated with mental health.

The project, which launched in October 2023, is an ongoing partnership. Designed to drive improvements in how colleges support student mental health and well-being, it builds on the Foundation's extensive work with colleges and universities across the U.S. to identify gaps in mental health resources and encourage initiatives to make student well-being a greater priority.

"Over the last decade, our Foundation has worked with colleges and universities to better understand where students are being supported and where important gaps remain," said Jay Ruderman, President of the Ruderman Family Foundation. "We partnered with The Princeton Review to build something that didn't exist before: a way to make student well-being visible and comparable across higher education, so it becomes a priority for institutions and for the families choosing them. Three years into the effort, we are encouraged by the progress we are seeing, but the ultimate measure of success will be whether institutions use what we are learning to make meaningful, lasting changes for their students."

The 2026 findings reported today are in two parts. The first reports on The Princeton Review's survey of administrators at 739 undergraduate institutions about their school's mental health and wellness services. The second reports on its survey of more than 56,000 students across 300 colleges about their awareness of those services. The full 2026 Campus Mental Health Services Survey Report is available for download and includes an executive summary, details on each survey and its methodology, survey questions and answer choices, and data analyses with year-over-year comparisons.

The growth in participation among schools suggests that comprehensive, campus-wide approaches to student mental health are no longer the exception; rather, they are increasingly becoming the norm among participating institutions. The Princeton Review and the Ruderman Family Foundation plan to evolve the project's Mental Health Services Honor Roll in 2027 to reflect that progress.

Year-over-Year Comparisons

Comparisons of survey findings—from the 2024 inaugural survey to the 2026 survey—show significant growth in many areas. Since the project's inception, institutional participation in the survey has nearly tripled from 250 participating institutions in 2024 to 540 in 2025 to 739 in 2026. Student participation has increased 409% from more than 11,000 students participating in the 2024 survey to more than 56,000 students participating in the 2026 survey. Finally, mental health education has become embedded in the academic curriculum. More than three quarters (77%) of institutions participating in the 2026 survey now offer for-credit or non-credit mental health and wellness education courses—compared with 58% so reporting in 2024.

Additional Findings of the 2026 Administrator Survey

Among the administrators at 739 institutions that completed the survey:

  • 99% (730) reported their colleges have a comprehensive mental health/wellness program that makes counseling, referral, and well-being services available to all students—up 41% from 515 so reporting in 2025, and up 238% from 216 so reporting in 2024
  • 99% (732) reported their colleges have a mental health services website—up 41% from 516 so reporting in 2025, and up 238% from 216 so reporting in 2024
  • 92% (371) reported their colleges have suicide prevention training programs—up 32% from 282 so reporting in 2025, and up 111% from 176 so reporting in 2024

Additional Findings of the 2026 Student Survey

Among the more than 56,000 students across 300 colleges that completed the survey:  

  • 82% agreed with the statement "If I needed to seek professional help for my mental or emotional health, I would know where to access my school's resources"—up from 79% so reporting on the 2025 survey
  • 80% agreed with the statement "Mental health services are readily available on campus"—up from 76% so reporting on the 2025 survey
  • 79% agreed with the statement "I am aware of mental health outreach efforts by my school"—up from 75% so reporting on the 2025 survey

Now in their second year, individualized benchmark reports give participating schools a comparison of their campus mental health services and programs with those of similar institutions and with the broader group of participating schools. The reports provide each school with a clear picture of where it stands and help translate the project's findings into meaningful, sustained action on campuses nationwide.

"We are deeply grateful to the Ruderman Family Foundation for its ongoing support for this project and its compelling advocacy for mental health and wellness services," said Rob Franek, Editor-in-Chief of The Princeton Review. "For more than 40 years, our company has helped millions of students find and get into their best-fit colleges. However—as many students, parents, and educators know—getting in is only the beginning. The road from orientation to graduation brings challenges across many fronts for which support is often essential, if not crucial. When it comes to student success in college, well-being is everything."

School Profiles & Honors

The project includes two initiatives to promote information about specific schools' campus mental health services and make that information accessible to college students, college applicants, parents, and student advisors.

  • The Princeton Review publishes information reported by administrators about their institution's campus mental health services in the company's profiles of the schools on its website and in its annual Best Colleges guide (now out in its 35th edition). Today, the company added campus mental health services information into the website profiles of the 739 institutions that participated in this year's survey. A list of the participating institutions is here.
  • A second annual initiative is the project's Mental Health Services Honor Roll. It recognizes schools that have demonstrated an exceptional commitment to their students' mental health and well-being. This year, 76 institutions earned this distinction—more than double the number (30) that made the Honor Roll in 2025 and more than four times the number (16) that made the Honor Roll in 2024. The list of schools that earned Honor Roll designations this year, and information about the criteria for the Honor Roll, is here.

Among the 76 schools named to the Mental Health Services Honor Roll this year, 11 hold the additional distinction of having been named to the Honor Roll for three consecutive years—in 2024, 2025 and 2026. In alphabetical order, they are:

Arizona State University

Boston University (MA)

Coastal Carolina University (SC)

Colorado State University

Columbia University (NY)

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

New York University

Princeton University (NJ)

State University of New York—University at Albany

University of North Carolina at Greensboro

William & Mary (VA)

Additional Presentations of Findings

  • Today, The Princeton Review posted a video on its popular YouTube channel featuring Rob Franek, the company's Editor-in-Chief, discussing the project's continuing mission and highlights of the 2026 survey findings.
  • On Wednesday, November 4, at 6:30 PM ET, The Princeton Review will host a webinar on the 2026 project titled "Advancing Campus Mental Health." Moderated by Rob Franek, the webinar will feature a panel of higher education leaders sharing their perspectives on the survey findings and the evolving state of campus mental health services. Information about registering for the webinar is here.

About The Princeton Review

The Princeton Review is a leading tutoring, test prep, and college admissions services company. Every year, it helps millions of college- and graduate school–bound students as well as working professionals achieve their education and career goals through its many education services and products. These include online and in-person courses delivered by a network of more than 4,000 teachers and tutors; online resources; a line of more than 150 print and digital books published by Penguin Random House; and dozens of categories of school rankings. Founded in 1981, the company is now in its 45th year. The company's Tutor.com brand, now in its 25th year, is one of the largest online tutoring services in the U.S. It comprises a community of thousands of tutors who have delivered more than 29 million tutoring sessions. The Princeton Review, headquartered in New York, NY, is not affiliated with Princeton University. For more information, visit PrincetonReview.com. Follow the company on Facebook (@ThePrincetonReviewSAT), Instagram (@theprincetonreview), LinkedIn (the-princeton-review), YouTube (@ThePrincetonReview), and TikTok (@princeton.review). Subscribe to The Princeton Review's twice-weekly newsletter, Brick & Mortarboard, here.

About the Ruderman Family Foundation

The Ruderman Family Foundation is an internationally recognized organization that works to end the stigma associated with mental health. The Foundation does this by identifying gaps in mental health resources and programs within the high school and higher education communities as well as by organizing other local and national programming and initiatives that raise greater awareness around the stigma. The Ruderman Family Foundation believes that inclusion and understanding of all people is essential to a fair and flourishing community and imposes these values within its leadership and funding. For more information, please visit www.rudermanfoundation.org

releases.title: Syngenta Awards Five Students the Durastak Traits of Tomorrow Scholarship
releases.body:
Program supports the next generation of leaders in their journeys toward careers in agriculture and STEM

RALEIGH, N.C., Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Syngenta awarded five college students $2,000 each through the Durastak Traits of Tomorrow Scholarship, a new program designed to support the success of the young adults building the future of agriculture.

The winners of the 2026 Durastak Traits of Tomorrow Scholarship are:

  • Sophia Barnum, Michigan State University, Crop and Soil Sciences
  • Braydon Binger, University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Agronomy
  • Kaarina Dunn, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Environmental Sciences and Agroecology
  • Ethan Fisher, Kansas State University, Biological Systems Engineering
  • Calvin Myers, Purdue University, Agribusiness Management

Recipients were selected by a panel of judges based on the merits of their applications and their demonstration of determination, resourcefulness and a forward-thinking mindset. The scholarship was open to seniors in high school or full-time students across the Midwest pursuing a degree in a science, technology, engineering, mathematics or agriculture-related field of study.

"We're proud to support the next generation of agricultural leaders with this scholarship opportunity," said Steve Sterchi, Head of Product & Commercial Strategy at Syngenta. "These five recipients are proof that the future of agriculture is in great hands, and we're excited to see the impact young people like them will make on the industry."

Scholarship recipient Ethan Fisher is studying agricultural engineering with the plan to start his own operation after graduation and help move the industry forward through the challenges it's facing today.

"Agriculture is an ever-changing world, it's never going to stop advancing, I don't think. It takes a lot to figure out how to build an operation from nothing nowadays and that's a task that I personally want to tackle," said Fisher. "Thank you for helping me cover my educational expenses, thank you for realizing that I want to be part of the solution here."

Another recipient, Kaarina Dunn, plans to pursue a career in agricultural policymaking at the state or national level to help farmers get the governmental assistance they need and teach young people about the importance of the agriculture industry.

"This scholarship shows youth that agriculture isn't something that just happens on a family farm, it happens in universities, it happens in classrooms all across the world," said Dunn. "I think hands-on agriculture work is obviously the way of the future. It's how youth learn about what they're eating every single day, where it comes from and how our local communities are impacted by the choices that we make in grocery stores."

To learn more about these recipients and see how Syngenta is committed to investing in the future of the agriculture industry, visit https://www.syngenta-us.com/seeds/corn-traits/durastak-scholarship.

releases.title: New Ipsos Survey Shows Risepoint-Supported Programs Continue to Deliver Strong ROI and Career Value for Learners
releases.body:
DALLAS, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Risepoint, a leading education technology company, today shared findings from a new Ipsos study showing a strong return on investment (ROI) for graduates of Risepoint-supported degree programs. Risepoint is an education technology company that helps regional universities launch and grow high-quality programs for modern learners in nursing, teaching, business, and other high-demand sectors. 

Amidst the continued national conversation around the cost and value of higher education, Risepoint commissioned its fourth annual ROI study with global research leader Ipsos. Ipsos surveyed 8,565 graduates of university partners supported by Risepoint. Graduates were working either full- or part-time both before and after completing their degree program.

The survey found that recent graduates of Risepoint-supported programs averaged low total tuition ($22,000), significant salary increases one year after graduation (+18 percent), and a short tuition payback period of 1.8 years. The study's results continue to reflect how the Risepoint model enables universities to deliver high-value, workforce-relevant programs that strengthen student outcomes and local communities.

Additional key findings from the 2026 Ipsos study include:

  • Graduates saw an even larger average salary increase (33 percent) three years after degree completion.



  • A majority (52 percent) funded their degrees without taking out any student loans.



  • An overwhelming majority of graduates (85 percent) agree their degree was worth the investment.



  • 78 percent of graduates would recommend their degree program to a friend or colleague.



  • The ability to continue working was the top reason for choosing online over on-campus or hybrid (59 percent), and 99 percent stayed employed during their program.



  • 89 percent agree that, because of their online degree, they were able to continue living and working in their local communities.

"As advances in AI and economic shifts fuel new questions about the future of work, modern learners need confidence that higher education will deliver practical, lasting value," said Fernando Bleichmar, CEO of Risepoint. "For the fourth consecutive year, these results prove that when regional universities offer flexible, high-demand programs, graduates achieve rapid payback, build meaningful careers, and strengthen their local communities. Risepoint remains deeply committed to helping our partner institutions expand access to education that genuinely pays off."

"What stands out in this research is the consistency of outcomes," said Chris Moessner, Executive Vice President at Ipsos. "From career growth and earnings to community impact, graduates of Risepoint-supported programs continue to study strong satisfaction with their investment in higher education. releases.title: Oklahoma Primary Aluminum and Tulsa Innovation Labs Host Three-Day Workforce Development Workshop on Preparing Regional Talent for 1,000+ High-Paying Jobs
releases.body:
Oklahoma State System of Higher Education Chancellor Sean Burrage welcomed educational and workforce leaders at Tulsa Tech to map talent pipelines and establish a local steering committee for the landmark primary aluminum project

TULSA, Okla., Oct. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Oklahoma Primary Aluminum, in partnership with Tulsa Innovation Labs, hosted a workforce development workshop at the Tulsa Tech Lemley Learning Center last week. The event convened local higher education, career tech, high school career counselors, workforce and community leaders to map talent pipelines, align curriculum and build clear employment pathways in support of the company's proposed state-of-the-art aluminum facility at the Tulsa Port of Inola.

Click here to view photos and videos from the workshop.

Chancellor Sean Burrage of the Oklahoma State System of Higher Education welcomed attendees to open the workshop, emphasizing the critical role of the state's educational institutions in preparing local talent for one of the largest economic development projects in Oklahoma history.

"We are standing on the threshold of a generational transformation," said Chancellor Sean Burrage. "Oklahoma Primary Aluminum is bringing an entirely new industry to our state, building the first primary aluminum facility in the United States since 1980. As educators and workforce leaders, our mission is to ensure Oklahomans are prepared, qualified and first in line for these life-changing career pathways."

Once operational, the 750,000-metric-ton facility will double current domestic primary aluminum production capacity, while creating 1,000 permanent direct jobs with average annual compensation of approximately $100,000. The workshop served as a critical operational milestone to ensure northeast Oklahoma's workforce is prepared to lead the world's most modern primary aluminum production facility. Discussions focused on modern aluminum manufacturing, projected job opportunities, career pathways and ways to align existing regional training programs with the facility's workforce needs, including:

  • Industry Overview: Local leaders were educated on modern primary aluminum manufacturing, including advanced, best-in-class technology and the full scope of industry operations and corporate roles.
  • Economic Multiplier: Attendees learned how OPA's direct jobs were part of a broader ecosystem expected to generate an average of 7,000 annual Oklahoma jobs across upstream and downstream suppliers, engineering partners and construction.
  • Job Family Deep-Dives: Technical review sessions covered diverse operational areas, from accounting, environmental and safety roles to technicians, operators and specialized metallurgists.
  • Targeted Career Pathways: Talent pipelines were explored for secondary students, current regional workers and university and graduate-level candidates.
  • Gap Analysis: Existing regional training programs, credentials and equipment were mapped against aluminum production requirements to identify opportunities for customized curriculum development.

"This workshop is a prime example of how our region comes together to turn transformative economic opportunities into real, lasting prosperity for local communities," said Kian Kamas, Interim Managing Director of Tulsa Innovation Labs. "By bringing together industry leaders, higher education and career tech institutions early in the process, we are ensuring that northeast Oklahoma builds a highly skilled talent pipeline ready to power the nation's most modern advanced manufacturing ecosystem."

Approximately 50 participants representing more than 12 academic and vocational institutions from northeast Oklahoma attended, along with workforce partners Madison Strategies Group and Good Jobs Initiative. The workshop concluded with the formation of a local steering committee and a schedule for ongoing discussions.

"Building the most modern primary aluminum facility in the country requires an equally forward-thinking workforce strategy," said Ziad Fares, Project Director for Oklahoma Primary Aluminum. "Although this is a new industry for the state, our long-term ambition is that every job is taken by an Oklahoman. We are grateful for our partnership with Tulsa Innovation Labs and our regional education partners, which allows us to build clear, accessible pathways for Oklahomans to secure high-paying, lifelong careers in advanced manufacturing."

About Tulsa Innovation Labs

Tulsa Innovation Labs is a tech-led economic development organization securing Tulsa's leadership in industries of the future and ensuring Tulsa remains a vibrant and influential hub of job creation and community engagement. They work with partners to help strengthen the region's key industries through programs and initiatives that catalyze capital and commercialization, talent and workforce, and place and infrastructure.

About Oklahoma Primary Aluminum

Oklahoma Primary Aluminum is a joint venture between Emirates Global Aluminium, the world's largest producer of premium aluminum, and Century Aluminum Company, the largest producer of primary aluminum in the United States. The company is planning a state-of-the-art primary aluminum production facility at the Tulsa Port of Inola in Rogers County, Oklahoma. Once operational, the facility is expected to produce 750,000 metric tons of primary aluminum annually once it starts production, more than doubling current U.S. primary aluminum production capacity while creating approximately 1,000 permanent jobs and thousands of construction jobs. The project represents a significant investment in strengthening America's domestic aluminum supply chain, supporting U.S. manufacturing, and advancing long-term economic growth. Learn more at oklahomaprimaryaluminum.com.

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Students are looking for more than endless choice from campus dining. They want food and experiences they can count on, options that fit the realities of their schedules and needs, and meaningful human connection along the way.
releases.title: Chartwells Higher Education's New Campus Voices Report Finds Students Want Dining They Can Trust
releases.body:
• New Campus Voices report explores the experiences, emotions and everyday realities behind student dining decisions
  • Findings are based on conversations with more than 2,000 students across 300 focus groups and 50 campuses
  • Students point to consistency, flexibility, functional wellness and authentic human connection as key parts of the dining experience

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Students are looking for more than endless choice from campus dining. They want food and experiences they can count on, options that fit the realities of their schedules and needs, and meaningful human connection along the way.

That is the central finding of Campus Voices, a new report released today by Chartwells Higher Education based on conversations with more than 2,000 students across 300 focus groups and 50 campuses, which explores the experiences, emotions and everyday realities behind student dining decisions, including what builds trust, what creates value and what brings students back.

"Campus Voices helps us understand the 'why' behind the data by listening directly to students," said Janelle Craft, VP of Insights and Innovation at Chartwells Higher Education. "Across these conversations, our students consistently described dining as something that needs to fit real life. They want reliable, quality meal options that reflect their needs and schedules, and experiences that feel responsive and human."

Direct, in-person feedback from students across diverse regions, campus sizes and dining models revealed five core themes driving student decision-making today:

  • Choice without confidence isn't really a choice. Having numerous options matters less to students if consistency and reliability are lacking. Trust in the quality and expectation of meals determines whether they are willing to champion dining options.
  • Variety is personal. Students report that variety, for them, is defined by the number of options that realistically fit their individual dietary needs, schedules and budgets. Customization serves as both a primary trust mechanism and a source of variety.
  • Value is an experience, not a price. Students evaluate meal value based on quality, completeness, convenience, flexibility and reliability. Perceived value is heavily influenced by balanced sides, fresh fruit and vegetables and thoughtful meal bundles.
  • Traditional mealtime is disappearing. Students no longer structure their days around traditional breakfast, lunch and dinner hours. Snacking and mobile pickups are increasing in popularity to meet students where they are.
  • The more digital dining becomes, the more human connection matters. Students report that while technology reduces operational friction, personal connections with dining staff and peers foster a sense of belonging on campus and make wait times feel shorter.

"Students want dining that fits their lives, but they also want to feel connected to the people and community around them," said Eva Wojtalewski, CEO of Chartwells Higher Education. "The food matters, but so does the welcome, the familiar face, and knowing that someone is paying attention. Their feedback is helping us create dining experiences that respond to the needs of each campus and help students feel seen."

Feedback from students shows that global flavors are now standard, and cuisine is judged based on how authentically it is prepared and how culturally appropriate the recipes are. Students also show strong demand for meals that are high in protein, minimally processed, and nutrient-rich so they feel energized and ready for their day. Campus dining events, including pop-ups, cultural celebrations and chef events, came up again and again as things students crave, and they make dining interactive, fostering valuable connections.

The findings will directly inform how Chartwells continues to evolve its menus, services and dining experiences across campuses, turning feedback into action. 

Campus Voices joins the 2026 Campus Dining Index and the Campus Dining Signal Report as part of Chartwells Higher Education's ongoing work to understand student perspectives and where expectations are headed.

Click here to download the full 2026 Campus Voices Report.

About Chartwells Higher Education  

Chartwells Higher Education, a part of Compass Group North America, is the recognized leader in contract foodservice management, hospitality, and guest service at more than 320 colleges and universities across the United States. Chartwells delivers "Dining, Made Personal" through quality, craveable food and dining programs tailored to each campus and designed around real student life. With signature service and meaningful connections, Chartwells partners with institutions to co-create campus experiences that make students and guests feel seen and welcomed.

releases.title: University of Phoenix highlights ways students can reduce college costs during National Transfer Student Week
releases.body:
Scholarships, transfer credits and prior-learning pathways help eligible students identify cost savings and affordability of degree completion

PHOENIX, Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix is recognizing National Transfer Student Week by highlighting the range of pathways that can help eligible students reduce education costs and make informed decisions about their educational journeys. Scholarships, transfer credits, prior learning assessments and alternative credit pathways offer students opportunities to gain insights about affordability and saving time and money on earning a degree while building on previous academic and professional achievements. 

"Many students assume affordability depends on a single scholarship or financial aid source," said Director of Financial Education Initiatives and Repayment Management, Chris Conway. "In reality, transfer credit, scholarship opportunities, prior learning and alternative credit pathways can work together to help reduce costs and create a more efficient path to degree completion. Understanding those options early can make a meaningful difference for students."

As University of Phoenix celebrates its 50th anniversary in 2026, the institution is reflecting five decades of helping working adults build on previous academic achievement and professional experience rather than start over. Today, transfer-credit pathways and scholarship opportunities remain an important part of that mission, helping eligible students reduce costs while pursuing degrees aligned with career goals.

Impact of Transfer-friendly programs

Affordable education pathways can help students continue pursuing their goals through life's most challenging seasons. For University of Phoenix transfer student Melonie Olipant, transfer credits helped her return to school after having children and continue making progress toward degree completion.

"Everyone expects a mother to say, 'I'm doing it for my children,' and they have always been a huge part of my why," Olipant said. "But there were moments when I was so tired, overwhelmed and lost that I didn't even know who I was doing it for anymore. I was so busy trying to hold everything together that I lost sight of myself.

"Still, I kept going not because I always felt strong, but because I refused to let the hardest season of my life become the ending of my story. Now, only a few credits away from my degree, I realize I wasn't just fighting for a better future for my children. I was fighting for myself, too. I didn't just earn a degree. I gave myself a future I once wasn't sure I'd see."

Scholarships help students reduce education costs

University of Phoenix offers multiple scholarship opportunities for eligible students like Olipant, ensuring that every new, qualifying student receives financial assistance. The Phoenix® Scholarship is available to students with at least three years of work experience, while the Transfer Scholarship is for those with 12 to 60 transfer credits.

  • Phoenix® Scholarship Savings Breakdown:

Bachelor's, Master's and Doctoral: Maximum value of $1K, provided the student maintains eligibility, applied over a set number of courses.

  • Transfer Scholarship Savings Breakdown:

Bachelor's: Maximum value of $3K, provided the student maintains eligibility, applied over 20 courses

In addition to University scholarships, alternate credit providers like Straighterline, Sophia and Study.com offer students an opportunity to earn general education credits via self-paced courses. Eligible students may complete general education courses with an alternative credit provider and then transfer eligible credits to University of Phoenix, helping them save time and money.

In addition to scholarships, transfer credit opportunities and alternate credit providers, University of Phoenix offers a comprehensive Savings Explorer® tool that presents information about scholarship opportunities, as well as transferring college credit and earning credit for prior learning through Prior Learning Assessment, national testing programs, alternative credit providers, and military service. By answering a few simple questions via the Savings Explorer tool, prospective students can find out what other students with relevant experience have saved.

University of Phoenix students and alumni have access to the Career Services for Life® commitment, helping to ensure the tools, resources, and support needed to thrive in their career of choice.

About University of Phoenix

University of Phoenix is Built for Real Life. 50 Years Strong. The University innovates to help working adults enhance their careers and develop skills in a rapidly changing world through flexible online learning, relevant courses, academic AI pillars, and skills-mapped curriculum for associate, bachelor's and master's degree programs. Active students and alumni have access to Career Services for Life® resources including career guidance and tools. For more information, visit phoenix.edu.

releases.title: WayUp Launches New Mobile App, Giving Students and Recent Grads a Faster Way to Catch Entry-Level Roles Before They Fill Up
releases.body:
CHICAGO, Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WayUp, the job search and recruiting marketplace built exclusively for college students and early-career job seekers, today announced the launch of its redesigned mobile app for iOS and Android. The app sends real-time alerts the moment a followed company posts a new internship or entry-level role, and lets candidates apply using the resume, education, and experience already saved to their WayUp profile, removing the need to rebuild an application from scratch for every role.

The launch comes as the market for early-career hires has tightened measurably: recent-college-graduate unemployment reached roughly 5.6% in the second quarter of 2026, among the highest readings in a decade outside the pandemic, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. With fewer no-experience entry-level openings available and employers moving quickly once applications start arriving, how fast a candidate sees and acts on a posting has become a meaningful factor in getting noticed.

"Right now, nearly half of entry-level jobs that used to require zero experience have disappeared, and recent grad unemployment just hit its highest point in a decade outside the pandemic," said Amy Farr-Jones, VP Growth at WayUp. "Students aren't losing out because they're not qualified—they're losing out because they see the role three days too late. We built the new WayUp app so the moment a great entry-level role opens, the right person sees it first and can move on it immediately."

The app is free to download and use, available now on the App Store and Google Play. Existing WayUp users can log in with their current account and keep their saved profile; new users can sign up directly in the app.

For more information, visit wayup.com.

About WayUp WayUp is a marketplace connecting college students and recent graduates with internships and entry-level jobs at companies ranging from startups to the Fortune 500. Candidates build a free profile and are matched to relevant openings, with employers able to reach out directly. WayUp also hosts Virtual Info Sessions connecting candidates with recruiters from companies including CVS Health, L'Oréal, and HSBC.

releases.title: New Survey Data Shows AI Reshaping College and Career Plans
releases.body:
HelloCollege data shows widespread AI use in coursework, rising career anxiety and shifting views on majors and degrees

OAK BROOK, Ill., Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HelloCollege today released findings from its 2026 College Student AI Survey, showing that AI is already shaping how college students learn, plan and think about their futures. The survey found that 66% of current college students are more concerned about their future career because of AI, 50% say AI has changed how they understand the use of a college degree and 82% use AI in their coursework.

The findings suggest students are not just experimenting with AI. They are incorporating it into everyday academic life while also weighing what it could mean for the long-term value of higher education. As AI becomes more common in the classroom, students are asking bigger questions about whether a degree will still deliver the career security and return on investment they expected.

That uncertainty is already influencing decision-making. More than 1 in 3 (37%) students say they are shifting their career plans around AI, showing AI is changing not only how students complete their work but also how they choose their path forward.

"AI is not some far-off thing for students," said Kevin Krebs, founder and CEO of HelloCollege. "It is already part of how they study, how they search for colleges and how they think about what comes after graduation. What this survey shows is that students see the value in AI, but they are also getting nervous about where they fit in. They are asking real questions about which majors still make sense, which careers feel safer and whether a college degree is going to give them the kind of return they expected in a job market that is changing fast."

Student sentiment in the survey reflects that uncertainty. Over half (58%) of college students believe AI is not a net good for society, with the biggest concerns being mass layoffs, difficulty telling truth from fiction, data privacy, learning loss and mass surveillance.

At the same time, students see potential upside, with 25% saying their biggest hope for AI is better work conditions through automation, followed by more free time and new fields of employment.

HelloCollege's full 2026 College Student AI Survey findings and methodology are available at www.sayhellocollege.com/blog/college-students-using-ai-statistics/. To learn more about HelloCollege or speak with a college counselor, visit sayhellocollege.com.

Founded in 2012 by Northwestern University alum and first-generation college graduate Kevin Krebs, HelloCollege is a national college counseling firm helping families navigate the admissions process with confidence. Through private counseling, workshops, and free resources, the company offers a team-based approach to college counseling, tutoring, essay coaching, and financial aid strategy. HelloCollege has guided more than 5,700 students to top universities and educated over 50,000 families nationwide, and it has been recognized by Forbes Advisor as one of the Best College Admissions Consultants of 2026 and rated Excellent on Trustpilot.

releases.title: College Promise and Los Angeles Community College District to Convene National Leaders at 2026 Careers Institute, Celebrate 10 Years of LA College Promise
releases.body:
Gathering at Los Angeles Trade-Technical College will focus on connecting Promise programs to high-demand careers and stronger regional economies

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- College Promise, in partnership with the Los Angeles Community College District (LACCD), will host the 2026 College Promise Careers Institute on Oct. 21–22, 2026, at Los Angeles Trade-Technical College, convening leaders from higher education, workforce, philanthropy, government, and industry around a central question: how Promise programs can move more learners into high-demand careers and strengthen regional economies. The Institute will also mark the 10th anniversary of LA College Promise, one of the nation's leading Promise programs and a 2025 College Promise National Impact Award honoree.

Under the theme Igniting Prosperity: The Path to Fueling Talent, Innovation, and Opportunity, sessions will cover:

  • Aligning Promise programs with regional workforce needs and employer demand
  • Artificial intelligence and the changing skills economy
  • Expanding opportunity for men and parenting students, building on College Promise's national student-father initiative
  • Communicating educational and economic outcomes, and return on investment, to policymakers, funders, and the public
  • Sustainable funding models that keep Promise programs strong for the long term

Launched in 2016 through a partnership among LACCD, the Los Angeles Unified School District, the City of Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, and philanthropic and community partners, LA College Promise is a model that has expanded educational opportunity for thousands of students demonstrating how coordinated community investment can help learners reach their potential and contribute to the region's economic future.

"Ten years ago, Los Angeles made a promise to its students, and LA Promise has spent the decade keeping it, showing firsthand the power of the Promise program idea," said Rosye Cloud, interim CEO of College Promise. "Across the country, that's hundreds of Promise programs giving students and families a real path to college and a career. It's helping community partners rethink how we connect education, workforce opportunity, and economic mobility. That's the life-changing work we're in Los Angeles to celebrate and build on at the Careers Institute."  

"Our LA Promise graduates feel like family to me. I have celebrated with them at commencement, listened to their stories, and watched them become the nurses, technicians, teachers, and entrepreneurs who power our city", said Dr. Alberto J. Román, LACCD Chancellor. "Ten years ago, Los Angeles made a promise to its young people that college would be within reach. Thousands of students have kept their end of that promise with courage and determination. Welcoming the Careers Institute to Los Angeles Trade-Technical College gives us the opportunity to share their success with the nation and recommit ourselves to the next generation of Promise scholars."

Today, the national College Promise movement includes more than 470 Promise programs serving communities in all 50 states. Together, these programs help learners earn credentials, connect to careers, and contribute to stronger local and regional economies and communities.

College Promise extends its gratitude to its National Advisory Board, National Leadership Council, national partners, philanthropies, and donors. Special thanks to the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, ECMC Foundation, The Kresge Foundation, The College Board, and CollegeAPP for their invaluable support.

About College Promise

College Promise is a national, nonpartisan nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing educational and economic opportunity by supporting Promise programs that increase college access, completion, and workforce success. Through research, policy leadership, technical assistance, and cross-sector partnerships, College Promise works to ensure that all learners have clear pathways to prosperity.

About the Los Angeles Community College District

The Los Angeles Community College District is the nation's largest community college district, serving hundreds of thousands of students annually through nine colleges. Through LA Promise, LACCD and its partners have expanded access to higher education by providing financial support, student success services, and pathways to degrees, certificates, transfer, and careers.

releases.title: Campus Launches Online Associate Degree in Cybersecurity Built for AI-Driven Threats
releases.body:
The two-year college's new degree includes preparation for CompTIA Security+, CEH, and AWS certifications, with live classes taught by experienced practitioners and university faculty that also teach at some of the nation's top colleges.

NEW YORK, October 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Campus, a two-year accredited college built for a generation of learners frustrated by the cost and pace of higher education, today announced the launch of its Associate of Science in Cybersecurity degree program. The program is designed to give students an affordable path into a four-year degree or a career in cybersecurity, equipping them with the skills they'll need to defend against increasingly sophisticated, artificial intelligence-driven threats.

AI is reshaping both how cyberattacks are carried out and the skills security teams need to respond. According to ISC2's 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 95% of cybersecurity professionals surveyed reported at least one skills gap on their team, and 73% said AI will create more specialized cybersecurity skills. In the new program, students learn the foundations of network security, threat detection, and ethical hacking, along with how to use AI in that work and defend against it when attackers do the same.

"Today's threats are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Attackers are already using AI to write phishing emails or make phone calls that sound exactly like a manager or family member," said Kaari Casey, Vice President of Academic Operations at Campus. "Entry-level IT professionals today must be able to catch that kind of deception quickly, and recognize when an AI tool's recommendation is wrong. Our students will develop the knowledge, skills, and judgment it takes to navigate this new world."

Building on the cybersecurity concentration Campus introduced within its Associate of Science in Information Technology in July, the program offers live, synchronous instruction taught by veteran cybersecurity practitioners and professors at top universities such as UC Davis, St. John's University, and University of Notre Dame. Over eight quarters, students move from introductory coursework in IT, cybersecurity, and AI to networking, cloud foundations, and IT ethics, then to network security, security operations and threat detection, and ethical hacking. AI runs through the curriculum: students learn to spot AI-generated deception in early security scenarios, validate AI-assisted recommendations in network-defense labs, and study how AI is used on both sides of an attack.

"Students in this program will build and test network defenses, work step by step through simulated incidents, and have to justify every decision they make. That rigor is what prepares students for the day-to-day work of an entry-level security role" said Casey.

Students also leave prepared for the high-value, industry-recognized certifications employers often look for in entry-level hires. Preparation for certification exams is built directly into students' coursework, which includes the content needed for students to sit for CompTIA's A+, Network+, Security+, and CySA+ exams, as well as the EC-Council Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) and AWS Cloud Practitioner and Solutions Architect certifications. Students who earn a B or higher in both their final course grade and final exam for a qualifying course are eligible for a Campus-funded certification exam voucher.

Students can apply starting now at campus.edu/online-cybersecurity-associate-degree. Classes will start in January 2027, with tuition set at $2,440 per quarter or $7,320 per academic year, including books and supplies.

As the first college built in the AI era, Campus is backed by entrepreneurs and investors including Sam Altman, Shaquille O'Neal, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, and 8VC, and is led by a board of respected former college presidents including John Wilson of Morehouse College and Gail Mellow of LaGuardia Community College. Campus delivers live, online classes taught by faculty who also teach at top colleges like Stanford and Howard. Campus' unique approach is grounded in a pioneering tech platform and a heavily-researched student success model proven to double two-year college graduation rates. Campus provides students with dedicated advisors, on-demand tutoring, and personalized coaching. Upon completion, students take skills learned in the program into the workforce or transfer to a growing number of four-year institution transfer partners.

About Campus

Campus is a new way to go to college, built for students looking for a lower-cost, faster launchpad into a career – or a four-year degree. Campus delivers live, online classes taught by professors who also teach at leading universities like Stanford and Howard University. The college's unique approach is grounded in a pioneering technology platform and a heavily-researched student success model that offers students dedicated advisors and on-demand tutoring and coaching to ensure their academic access. Campus was named one of Fast Company's Most Innovative Companies. To learn more, visit campus.edu.

releases.title: College Student Mental Health: New AllOne Health Research Reveals Who Seeks Counseling and How They Access Care
releases.body:
Peer-reviewed research examines 2,800 counseling cases across 36 higher education institutions, revealing how students access support for mental health, relationship concerns, and everyday stress.

WILKES-BARRE, Pa., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Anxiety, depression, and grief were the leading reasons college students sought counseling through AllOne Health's Student Assistance Program (SAP), with mental health concerns accounting for 61% of cases, according to a pair of peer-reviewed studies published in the Journal of Education and Human Development. Students also reached out for help with personal relationships (19%) and everyday life stress (17%).

The research, announced today by AllOne Health, a leading provider of Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs), Student Assistance Programs (SAPs), and integrated whole health solutions, gives university presidents, student affairs professionals, healthcare service providers, and other campus leaders a data-driven view of what brings students to counseling, how quickly they connect with care, and how a Student Assistance Program can complement campus services.

"Today's college students bring a wide range of life experiences, schedules, and needs. Student Assistance Programs give institutions an innovative way to meet them," said Keith Wasley, President & CEO of AllOne Health. "When a student reaches out, fast access to high-quality clinical care and in-the-moment support makes the biggest impact. Our SAP is designed to complement campus student services by giving students a trusted place to turn, 24/7, by phone, app, or video."

What Brings Students to Counseling

The counseling study analyzed 2,800 cases from 36 colleges and universities across the United States between 2020 and 2024, examining why students sought support, how counseling was delivered, and how they used services. Students who used counseling represented a broad range of ages and life stages. Key findings include:

  • Mental health was the leading concern. Mental health issues accounted for 61% of cases, including anxiety (23%), depression and mood disorders (11%), grief and loss (5%), and other emotional issues (22%).
  • Relationships and everyday stress were also common. Personal relationship concerns accounted for 19% of cases, and personal life stress accounted for 17%.
  • Counseling was delivered almost entirely by video or phone. Based on the 1,986 cases with recorded modality, online video accounted for 89% of cases, telephone counseling for 10%, and in-person counseling for 1%.
  • Nearly 1 in 4 cases were resolved in a single session. Students used an average of 3.5 sessions over 47 days, and 24% of cases used just one session of counseling to resolve the student's concern.
  • The length of care varied with student needs. The largest share of cases used 2 or 3 sessions (42%), and about a third (34%) used 4 to 9 sessions, with sessions spaced about 18 days apart on average.
  • Students represented a broad range of ages. 27% of clients were of traditional undergraduate age (18 to 24), while 33% were 25 to 29 years old, 26% were in their 30s, and 14% were 40 to 75 years old.

Why It Matters for Higher Education

Among students who used the program, mental health concerns were the most common reason for seeking support, followed by relationship difficulties and everyday stress. With counseling available by video or phone, students can connect with care around their classes, work, and family responsibilities, when and where they need it.

"Through our partnerships with colleges and universities, AllOne Health's Student Assistance Program has been extending the reach of campus counseling centers, providing additional licensed clinical support aligned with each institution's student mental health initiatives, goals, and services," said Jason C. McDaniel, Regional Vice President of Operations at AllOne Health and co-author of the studies. "With nearly a quarter of cases in our study resolved in a single session, focused counseling helps our partner institutions support more students with the resources they already have."

Fast, Flexible Access When Students Reach Out

During intake, 11% of cases included a brief "In-the-Moment" telephone support call, and across the five-year study period, the first call was answered in about 16 seconds on average. Students most often began their requests for counseling by phone (70%) or through the mobile app (30%), both available 24/7.

"Students use counseling for many reasons, ranging from anxiety and depression to relationship difficulties and personal stress, and this mix differs slightly by age as well," said Mark Attridge, Ph.D., co-author of the study. "Understanding why and how students use counseling can help institutions consider the support resources needed by students in different age groups."

Practical Support for Daily Life

A companion study examined 5,604 work/life service cases among students at 29 colleges and universities. Personal life and convenience support accounted for 44% of those cases, followed by financial referrals (36%), legal referrals (12%), and childcare assistance (4%). Students used personal life concierge support at three times the rate of employees using AllOne Health's EAP work/life services over the same period (44% vs. 14%). Together, the two studies show how Student Assistance Programs can complement campus services by giving students access to both counseling and practical resources for real-life problems.

"The purpose of this research was to develop a clearer profile of students who use Student Assistance Program services, including the concerns that bring them to counseling and how they access support," said Dr. Attridge. "By documenting these service-use patterns and comparing them with existing research on campus counseling center users, we can better understand the role of external SAP services."

About the Research

The studies describe service utilization among AllOne Health program users. The samples were not designed to represent all college students in the United States, measure changes in student well-being or academic outcomes, or establish the effectiveness of a particular service model. The work-life study sample was especially concentrated among students attending large, private, for-profit institutions and fully online or hybrid schools.

Both studies were authored by Mark Attridge, Ph.D., M.A., of Attridge Consulting, Inc., and Jason C. McDaniel, LCSW, CEAP, MBA, of AllOne Health, and published in the Journal of Education and Human Development in March 2026. Dr. Attridge, an independent research consultant, was engaged by AllOne Health to conduct the studies. McDaniel is an AllOne Health executive.

releases.title: From Raider to Bronco: GRCC, WMU to Guarantee Admission for Transfer Students
releases.body:
New Bronco Bound partnership offers a direct path to a bachelor's degree, guaranteed scholarships and more

GRAND RAPIDS, Mich., Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A GRCC Raider today. A WMU Bronco tomorrow. For Grand Rapids Community College students dreaming of earning a bachelor's degree, that next step is about to become a lot more certain.

Through a new partnership called the Bronco Bound Guarantee, students who earn an associate degree at GRCC will be guaranteed admission to Western Michigan University, along with an annual scholarship ranging from $1,000 to $4,500 for eligible students.

Leaders from both institutions will make the partnership official during a signing ceremony at 3 p.m. Friday, Oct. 16, at GRCC's Applied Technology Center, Secchia Piazza, on the college's main campus in Grand Rapids. Media are invited to attend.

"Strong partnerships create strong pathways for students. This agreement reflects a shared commitment to making higher education more accessible, affordable and connected," said GRCC President Dr. Kathryn A. Rogalski. "We are proud to partner with Western Michigan University, an institution that recognizes the quality of a GRCC education and the strong foundation our students bring to their next chapter. Together, we are creating more opportunities for students to achieve their educational goals and build a brighter future for themselves and our communities."

The Bronco Bound Guarantee is designed to take some uncertainty out of transferring from community college to a four-year university.

"Having led a community college, I know the important role these institutions play in helping students discover their potential and pursue their goals," said WMU President Russ Kavalhuna.

"Our partnership with Grand Rapids Community College builds on that foundation. We want students to arrive at Western knowing they belong here, find opportunities to put their learning into practice and have the support to thrive, graduate, and build meaningful careers."

In addition to guaranteed admission, qualifying GRCC students will have their WMU application fee waived and receive scholarship consideration automatically, with eligible students guaranteed an annual award of $1,000 to $4,500.

Students will also have access to dedicated transfer advising and recommended academic plans to help them make the most of their credits. Those who can complete an associate degree through an approved transfer guide or program agreement will have their defined credits apply toward the corresponding WMU degree requirements, avoiding the frustration of losing credits along the way.

And students won't have to wait until their first day at WMU to begin feeling like Broncos.

Prior to admission, eligible students will enjoy early access to university resources and campus experiences, including free admission to WMU sporting events, excluding hockey.

The partnership is about more than providing a route to admission. It is also about helping students make a successful transition into university life, connect with the Bronco community and take advantage of distinctive academic programs and experiential learning opportunities.

The partnership also recognizes the importance of completing a GRCC credential. Through a no-cost reverse transfer process, students who continue their education at WMU can have eligible university credits transferred back to GRCC to help them earn an associate degree.

GRCC and WMU will continue working together beyond the signing ceremony, with WMU participating in at least one transfer-focused event each semester and both institutions reviewing student enrollment and achievement data to strengthen the partnership.

For GRCC students, Bronco Bound means the journey toward a bachelor's degree can begin with greater confidence, knowing their next opportunity is already within reach.

About Grand Rapids Community College

GRCC was established in 1914 — Michigan's first community college — and is focused on making college education accessible and affordable. Classes are scheduled weekdays, evenings and Saturdays in Grand Rapids, Holland and online. We offer traditional liberal arts and occupational career pathways, adult education courses and skilled training courses and apprenticeships.

About Western Michigan University

WMU students are individuals who are truly unique. At Western, we celebrate the passions that drive students and the possibilities that inspire them. For us, a degree is a pursuit of purpose where students are empowered to learn and where an experience-driven education leads to a meaningful career. Broncos prosper. Nine out of 10 graduates are employed quickly, working in their field in jobs they like. WMU students make their mark on the world—Grammy recipients, Super Bowl champions, doctors, teachers, pilots and countless others have flourished here. Western is the place where students become the best version of themselves. WMU is a public research university, offering a range of undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral programs to more than 17,000 students. Learn more at https://wmich.edu/
